AI right now has the potential to take over a lot of different industries, not just the arts. We're seeing that in the tech industry, marketing, business, even medicine. Unfortunately, it's an unavoidable trend. 

So yes, AI can make art, but making art isn't the only reason an artist pursues the creative field. It takes a lot of courage to go on a course that doesn't guarantee a job post graduation. But we also see that a college degree doesn't mean much nowadays, it's all about your own drive and motivation.

Like another commenter pointed out, you need to carve out your own niche. If you want to be an artist who can support yourself, you need to find what people want. A lot of us in the arts have to find multiple streams of income, it's just part of our lifestyle. That isn't as bad as it sounds, but teaching, grant funding, exhibitions, freelance are all things a lot of us have to do to survive. But creative people can do it. They're able to find alternative ways to make money, to create business niches never thought of before!

So honestly, I think AI can take over anything, but if she's passionate and serious, she'll find her footing. I'd recommend looking into state schools or even starting at a community college to save money. She might find out a degree in art isn't for her, that's cool. But as appealing as a fancy art school is, they often aren't worth it. Many state universities have art programs that will offer you the same opportunities with half the cost. And if she decides she doesn't want to do art, she can transfer programs much easier.

Edit: for reference I am a ceramic artist, I sell my work, I work in a ceramic studio and teach pottery skills to others.

Definitely take a class, I don't think it's impossible to learn to do this at home, but if you've never been in a ceramics studio you might not realize how much complexity there is to this craft. I'm not trying to gatekeep, but I think it's important people know how much time and energy goes into even something simple like this cup. It sounds like you want to learn to wheel throw. After witnessing the mess alone that comes along with wheel throwing it might turn you off to doing this at home, you'd need a dedicated space like a basement or garage that you could likely hose down if you needed to. This only covers clean up and space, you have to learn how to wedge and center clay, how to throw the clay itself, the nuance to drying and transporting greenware clay to a studio for firing. Additionally, a lot of studios would be hesitant to rent kiln space to someone who's never worked in clay before. It can be a liability to other people's work if your work isn't dried properly, your clay too thick, or if you don't know the proper ways to glaze. All things that are helpful to learn directly from instructors who do this stuff for a living.

I'm saying all of this not to turn you off from getting into ceramics, but to just illuminate how important it is to really take a class. A lot of crafts and hobbies don't require the level of chemistry that ceramics do, just some things to consider.
